title: What You Lose When You Stop Reading Physical Books
author: Jasna HodžiI
source: Big Think Books on Substack (bigthinkbooks.substack.com), July 9, 2026
summary: After years of reading almost exclusively on the Libby app, Jasna HodžiI abandons a good e-book to finish a print paperback a friend handed her at an airport, and finds the act strangely significant. To understand her 'print renaissance' she interviews linguist Naomi Baron, who reframes the difference not as mystical but as measurable and behavioral: readers report focusing better, feeling more transported, and becoming more emotionally involved with characters in print, while describing digital reading mainly in terms of convenience and cost. Baron explains that people read faster digitally, re-read less, and are less absorbed — differences we cannot reliably feel, which is exactly why they are worth knowing. The essay resists a simple print-versus-digital verdict: Baron's practical rule is to read in print what you want to ponder and read digitally what is a 'one-off' or serves your situation, keeping both formats open and using each where it delivers the most value.
points: Physical books are singular, self-contained objects — a specific weight, cover, and feel — while phones and e-readers are 'portals,' insubstantial panes of glass that look like every other device.
Surveys across countries find readers value the physicality of print and call it 'real reading,' and describe feeling more emotionally involved and transported than with digital books.
People read faster digitally, re-read less, and look things up less; they assume speed is good, but the slower pace of print gives a story more time to 'simmer.'
Books carry meaning beyond their text — margin notes, gifts, and collections become a reflection of who we are, and browsing physical shelves surfaces serendipitous discoveries an algorithm won't.
Baron rejects a blanket verdict: choose the medium by your goal — print to ponder or absorb a novel, digital for one-off reading, travel, textbooks, or learning a new language.
quotes: Most people understand that there is something they do when reading in print that they don’t do when reading digitally,” Naomi Baron told me.
Despite the rise of digitization, humans don’t want to give up tangible items,” Baron said.
They are less singular objects than portals, panes of fingerprint-smeared glass revealing a million different functions.
What do you gain by being able to browse and handle physical books that you don’t get when you’re browsing some poorly designed algorithm on Amazon?” Baron asked.
When people hold onto books or collect libraries, I interpret that behavior to mean, ‘These books are part of who I am now,’” explained Baron.
And that’s kind of the point: If we can’t feel the difference, that’s precisely why the pattern is worth knowing.
It’s figuring out how to keep both formats open, and use each one where it actually delivers the most value.
